build-vs-buy.title: Somebody is stealing with our checkout
build-vs-buy.concept: Build vs buy: build what differentiates you, buy what has become a commodity, and count the costs neither invoice shows.
build-vs-buy.voice: Every vendor demo ends with the same slide: 'and it just works'. Note who built the slide.
build-vs-buy.briefing: Q1 of Year 3, about 28 engineers. Chargebacks have tripled in two quarters and a fraud ring has discovered our seller onboarding. An auditor arrives next quarter and will want to know how we decide which payment is fraud.
build-vs-buy.dilemma: Is stopping fraud something Mercadito should be good at, or something it should pay someone else to be good at?
build-vs-buy.disagreement: Experts disagree here. Wardley-style mapping says fraud scoring is a commodity by now, so buy it and spend people on what differentiates; others argue that in a marketplace the fraud patterns are the business (seller collusion, fake listings) and outsourcing them outsources what you most need to learn. Both are right about some marketplace.
build-vs-buy.readNext: Start with the chapter of Wardley Maps on evolution (genesis, custom, product, commodity), then reread the innovation-token essay as a budget for what you build, and finish with Team Topologies on what a new domain costs a team's head.

build-risk.title: Build it: a risk district with fraud-service and its own data
build-risk.optimizes: Control over the rules and the data; a capability competitors cannot buy.
build-risk.costs: A team for two quarters, worse detection before better, and every control is yours to prove.

buy-scoring.title: Buy it: a fraud-scoring vendor called from checkout
buy-scoring.optimizes: Live in weeks, with fraud signals from thousands of other merchants.
buy-scoring.costs: A fee on every order, a black box in the checkout path, and a contract that renews on their terms.

hybrid-rules.title: Buy the score, own the rules: vendor plus a fraud-rules module
hybrid-rules.optimizes: Commodity scoring bought, marketplace-specific judgement kept in-house.
hybrid-rules.costs: Two things to run, a seam between them, and still an invoice.

events.vendor-price-change: Renewal letters arrive. 'To keep investing in our platform', every vendor's price goes up.
events.audit-requirement: The auditor's first request list: 140 items, including 'evidence of fraud control design and operating effectiveness'.

inspections.chargeback-spreadsheet: Site inspection: chargeback disputes live in a shared spreadsheet with 900 rows and two owners. The auditor will ask who approved row 412.

review.what-differentiates: Is fraud detection where Mercadito differentiates, or a commodity it happens to need? Where on the map is it?
review.hidden-costs: What does this choice cost that will not show up on the first invoice or in the first sprint?
review.when-switch: What price, volume or audit finding would make you cross to the other side, and how would you notice?

rubric.grounded-context: The context names the constraints that shaped the choice (team, orders, chargebacks, the audit, cash).
rubric.names-evolution: The decision says whether fraud detection differentiates Mercadito or is a commodity, and builds or buys accordingly.
rubric.names-hidden-cost: The consequences name a cost neither side advertises: fees that scale, lock-in, people to run it, evidence for the auditor.
rubric.names-given-up: What was given up is written down in a full sentence.
rubric.revisit-trigger: The trigger to switch sides is a condition someone could notice, not a hope.

buildVsBuy.buildTakesATeam: A useful in-house fraud service takes four or five engineers about two quarters, out of roughly 28; that is most of a team's roadmap.
buildVsBuy.buildNewDistrict: A new service, its own database and a synchronous call from checkout: one more deployable and one more contract to keep.
buildVsBuy.buildSalaries: Five salaries and a new database cost more this year than a vendor's fees would at today's volume.
buildVsBuy.buildNewDomain: Fraud is a domain of its own (features, labels, false positives, disputes); someone has to learn it before they can own it.
buildVsBuy.buildColdStart: A model trained only on Mercadito's own history starts blind to fraud patterns it has not seen yet, so early detection is worse than a vendor's.
buildVsBuy.buildLearnsMarketplace: After about two quarters of labelled chargebacks, rules tuned to seller collusion and fake listings catch what generic scoring misses.
buildVsBuy.buildEvidenceOwnControls: Building it means the auditor audits it: model change logs, access reviews and override records are ours to produce.
buildVsBuy.buildNoInvoiceToReprice: With no per-transaction fraud fee, a vendor repricing touches less of the cost base.
buildVsBuy.buyLiveInWeeks: Integrating a fraud-scoring API is a few weeks for two engineers; scoring is a product now, not a research project.
buildVsBuy.buyConsortiumData: A vendor sees fraud across thousands of merchants, so it recognises stolen cards and devices on the first day.
buildVsBuy.buyCheckoutDependency: Every checkout now waits on a third party; timeouts need a fallback decision (approve, decline, or queue for review).
buildVsBuy.buyBlackBox: Support and risk analysts get a score without a reason; explaining a declined seller to that seller gets harder.
buildVsBuy.buyFeePerOrder: The fee is a few cents per scored transaction; at Year 3 growth it outgrows a small team's salary within a year.
buildVsBuy.buyLockedInAtRenewal: After a year, our labels, thresholds and workflows live in their dashboard. Switching means re-integrating and re-tuning, so the price increase gets signed.
buildVsBuy.buyAttestationHelps: The vendor's own attestation covers most of the model; we still evidence how we use the score and who overrides it.
buildVsBuy.hybridRulesTakeAPair: A rules module with a dozen marketplace-specific rules takes two engineers about a quarter, on top of the integration.
buildVsBuy.hybridScorePlusLocal: Vendor scoring catches generic card fraud; our rules catch the patterns only a marketplace sees, like a seller buying from themselves.
buildVsBuy.hybridSeam: Rules first, vendor second, and a policy for when they disagree: a seam that needs its own tests.
buildVsBuy.hybridTwoThingsToRun: Two systems decide on the same payment. When a good customer is declined, someone has to find out which one said no.
buildVsBuy.hybridFilteredFee: Rules can skip the vendor for clearly safe and clearly fraudulent orders, so the fee lands on fewer transactions, but it still lands.
buildVsBuy.hybridRulesCompound: Once the rules module exists, product teams ship new risk checks without a vendor ticket.
buildVsBuy.hybridLeverageAtRenewal: Owning the rules and the labels makes switching vendors credible, so the renewal is a negotiation rather than a notice.
buildVsBuy.hybridTwoControlSets: Two control sets to evidence: the vendor's attestation plus our rules' change history and approvals.
buildVsBuy.vendorsReprice: In Year 3 vendors that priced for growth start pricing for margin; most contracts renew a few points higher.
buildVsBuy.auditFieldwork: An audit takes weeks of engineers' time collecting evidence, plus the auditors' own fee.
buildVsBuy.auditChangeControl: Formal change approval adds a step to every production release; it slows delivery more than it prevents incidents.
